stem: A random variable X takes values 1, 2, 3, 4 with P(X = k) = k/10 for k = 1, 2, 3, 4. Given that X >= 2, what is the conditional probability P(X <= 3 | X >= 2)?

per_option_rationale.rationale: 5/10 = P(2<=X<=3) without dividing by P(X>=2); the student forgets to condition and reports the unconditional probability.
5/8 arises from computing P(2<=X<=3)/P(X>=3) using P(X>=3)=7/10 but miscounting the denominator as 8/10.
3/5 = 6/10 comes from treating P(X<=3) = (1+2+3)/10 = 6/10 and ignoring the conditioning on X>=2 entirely.

explanation_sections.punchline: Conditioning shrinks the sample space to X>=2; within that space P(X<=3) is 5 out of 9 probability mass.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify model: conditional probability on a discrete PMF. Decisive move: apply P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Event A = {X<=3}, Event B = {X>=2}, so A and B = {2<=X<=3} = {X=2, X=3}. Compute numerator = 2/10+3/10=5/10. Compute denominator = 2/10+3/10+4/10=9/10. Divide: 5/9. Hidden trap: do not use P(X<=3) in the numerator; the conditioning truncates the range at 2, so X=1 is excluded.
explanation_sections.lesson: In conditional probability on a discrete RV, the numerator is the intersection, not the unconditional probability of the first event.
explanation_sections.timing: 120 seconds. Trap: using P(X<=3)=6/10 unconditionally to get 3/5. Trap: forgetting to divide by P(X>=2) and reporting 5/10.
